defaults.permitted_development: Across East Sussex, driveway surfacing is often permitted development, but the easy route usually depends on drainage. If the area in front of the house and facing the highway exceeds 5 square metres, it should be permeable or direct run-off to a permeable part of the curtilage, and any dropped kerb is dealt with separately.

rules.height_rules: Across East Sussex, driveway projects are rarely judged by surface height alone. The problem usually arises where the scheme changes levels significantly through ramps, retaining walls, terracing or raised parking areas.
rules.depth_rules: Across East Sussex, no set driveway depth applies, but the parking space should work in practice: vehicles should be able to sit within the curtilage rather than project over the pavement. Tight frontage layouts often fail on useability before they fail on surfacing rules.
rules.boundary_rules: Across East Sussex, boundary treatment is often the decisive issue on a driveway scheme. Opening the frontage to vehicles can affect sightlines, front walls, verges and street character even where the paving itself looks straightforward.
rules.roof_rules: Across East Sussex, driveways have no roof-specific permitted development rule. If the scheme also adds a car port, canopy or garage-style cover, that structure is assessed separately from the surfacing.
rules.materials_rules: Across East Sussex, the easiest driveway material strategy is usually one that handles water on site rather than sending it to the road. Broad impermeable paving on a front garden is much more likely to create a planning issue than permeable or well-drained surfacing.

restrictions.conservation_area: A new or enlarged driveway in a conservation area often gets closer scrutiny if it replaces soft landscaping or alters a traditional frontage.
restrictions.listed_building: Listed building consent may be needed where driveway works alter the setting or fabric of a listed building, including boundary features and historic surfacing.
restrictions.article4_notes: Where Article 4 directions or planning conditions bite, a driveway that would usually fall within householder rights can still need planning permission.

rules.permitted_development: In Hastings, the usual householder route for a driveway is strongest where the works stay within the plot and surface-water run-off is handled properly. Frontage parking areas over 5 square metres generally need permeable surfacing or drainage to a porous area, and a new vehicular crossing remains a separate highways matter.

rules.height_rules: A driveway does not have a simple national height limit, but raised platforms, retaining edges and stepped level changes can still turn a straightforward surfacing job into a planning issue.
rules.depth_rules: There is no fixed national depth limit, but the layout should leave enough space for vehicles to stand within the site instead of overhanging the footway. Front garden schemes are easiest to defend when drainage and manoeuvring have been solved together.
rules.boundary_rules: Driveway works should stay within the curtilage, but widening an opening onto the road, crossing a verge or footway, or removing a front wall can trigger separate highway or planning issues. Visibility at the access often matters more than the paving choice on its own.
rules.roof_rules: There is no roof allowance for a driveway in itself. Any canopy, covered bay or car-port element proposed with the parking area needs to be checked as a separate structure.
rules.materials_rules: Choose materials with drainage in mind, not only appearance. For front driveway areas over 5 square metres, the normal householder route usually depends on permeability or on-site discharge to a porous area within the curtilage.

restrictions.conservation_area: In conservation areas, removing planting or historic front-boundary features to create parking can trigger a closer review even where the surfacing itself seems minor.
restrictions.listed_building: If the proposal serves a listed building, removing walls, gates, paving or other curtilage features can trigger listed building consent as well as planning checks.
restrictions.article4_notes: Article 4 directions or planning conditions can remove normal householder rights for hard surfacing, frontage parking or boundary alterations.
